title: Chicken Karaage (Japanese)
description:
What is striking about the Japanese relationship with fried chicken is the frequency of consumption—more often
than a once-in-a-while indulgence. In America, eating fried chicken every day is viewed as gluttonous behavior.
The same practice in Japan is met with gentler judgment. Their style of fried chicken is called karaage
(pronounce kara-ah-geh), sometimes known as tatsuta-age. The Japanese may have fine-tuned the art of chicken
frying better than any culinary culture. (Alex Talbot, who co-wrote a terrific culinary science book called Ideas In
Food, began using potato starch for his fried chicken because it is our new best friend… “[it’s] extremely light
and holds its crispness for hours. Yes, hours. I didn’t think our fried chicken could get better.”) You could also
make this with any “American” KFC-like flavorings, rather than the Asian ones.
ingredients: 8 chicken thighs (boneless skinless, or just boneless)
4 cups duck fat (or vegetable oil), enough to fill a pan 2 inches deep
directions: Using a sharp knife, poke the thighs with the point a number of times on both sides. Then, cut the thighs
into 4 or more good bite-sized chunks. Place the chicken in a shallow pan and set aside.
For the marinade, combine garlic, ginger, soy sauce, mirin, sesame oil, and a few grinds of black pepper in
a bowl and mix. Pour marinade over chicken and coat well using your hands. There should be just enough
marinade to coat the chicken. Cover and refrigerate at least 20 minutes or up to two hours.
Heat six cups duck fat (or vegetable oil) in a heavy-bottomed pot over medium-high heat until the oil
reaches 320 degrees Fahrenheit. Pour off extra marinate, then mix in the beaten egg. Dredge each piece in
the 1 cup potato starch and gently toss until lightly coated. Carefully lower the chicken pieces into the hot
oil, without overcrowding. Cook the chicken until the flour starts to set and gets some color, 1-2 minutes,
turning once, then remove to a paper towel or rack.
Heat the oil to 360 and cook the pieces until nicely browned, 1-3 minutes more, with some turning. Once
the chicken is cooked through, remove it to the tray or rack. Toss with a pinch of kosher salt while still
hot. Repeat next batch.
Serve immediately with lemon wedges and Japanese Kewpei mayonnaise (or add a little rice vinegar and
MSG to regular mayo).
Bonus step
When finished deep-frying the chicken, season with salt, then sprinkle with this soy-chili oil vinaigrette:
1/2 cup Japanese soy sauce
1/4 cup rice vinegar
2 tsp. hot chili oil
2 tsp. sugar
Combine all ingredients and stir until sugar is dissolved.
